Design and RTL-to-GDSII Implementation of a Gate-All-Around Nanosheet CMOS Inverter Using the Cadence Flow in a Virtualized Workstation Environment

M. Nisha Angeline, Professor and Head
Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Velalar College of Engineering and Technology, Thindal, Erode, Tamil Nadu, India
Corresponding author: M. Nisha Angeline
Abstract

Gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors replace the FinFET at the 3-nm node because a gate that fully wraps a stack of thin channels restores electrostatic control at gate lengths near 14 nm and lets the designer tune drive current continuously through sheet width. This paper reports a complete, reproducible cell-to-chip design of a GAA nanosheet CMOS inverter (INV_GAA_X1) using the Cadence design platform running inside a VMware Workstation guest. The device is modelled with the industry-standard BSIM-CMG multi-gate compact model at a generic 3-nm-class rule set (gate length 14 nm, contacted gate pitch 48 nm, three 5-nm sheets, 6-track 168-nm cell). Schematic and transient characterisation use Virtuoso and Spectre; the physical cell is built in Virtuoso Layout and streamed to Calma GDSII; and the same cell is carried through a register-transfer-level (RTL) to GDSII flow with Genus synthesis and Innovus place-and-route. A dependency-free GDSII stream writer and a calibrated reference compact model, both released with the paper, let the layout and the electrical figures be regenerated and checked outside the licensed tools. At VDD = 0.7 V the reference model gives a switching threshold of 350 mV, a maximum voltage gain of 28, noise margins of 255/266 mV, a fan-out-of-4 propagation delay of 5.77 ps and 0.84 fJ per cycle in a 0.0161 µm² footprint, a 16 % delay and 17 % area reduction over a 5-nm-class FinFET inverter evaluated with the same model, and an 11-stage fan-out-of-3 ring oscillator built from the cell runs at 12.1 GHz (3.77 ps per stage). A NAND2 cell built with the N and P sheet widths swapped balances its series stack in a 3-pitch, 0.0242 µm² footprint with a 7.60-ps worst-case FO4 delay, and a 0.0207 µm² six-transistor SRAM bitcell whose sheet-width ratios raise the read static noise margin to 105 mV against 94 mV for a one-fin FinFET cell of the same area. Every delivered GDSII is DRC-clean against a 26-rule nanosheet deck, LVS-matched to its schematic and extracted to SPEF, and post-layout simulation with the extracted RC gives a fan-out-of-4 delay of 8.42 ps; the inverter stream the inverter stream passes independent read-back with 32 boundaries on 11 layers and four pin texts. The methodology is intended as a reference for research groups adopting GAA technology in academic environments where the EDA tools run on virtualised infrastructure.

Index terms: gate-all-around, nanosheet FET, BSIM-CMG, CMOS inverter, GDSII, RTL-to-GDSII, Cadence Virtuoso, Genus, Innovus, VMware Workstation, 3-nm technology node.

I.Introduction

The FinFET carried CMOS from the 22-nm to the 5-nm node, but its electrostatics are set by fin quantisation: drive strength can only be changed in integer fin counts, and at gate lengths below about 16 nm the fin must be so thin that variability and mobility degrade [1], [2]. The gate-all-around nanosheet transistor answers both limits. The channel is a vertical stack of thin silicon sheets, each surrounded on all four sides by the high-k/metal gate, so short-channel control is set by sheet thickness rather than fin width, while the effective width can be tuned continuously through the lithographically defined sheet width [1], [3]. Samsung's 3-nm Multi-Bridge-Channel FET (MBCFET) [3], Intel's RibbonFET and the IBM/Samsung nanosheet demonstrations [1] make GAA the mainstream device of the 3-nm and 2-nm nodes, and the IRDS roadmap projects stacked-nanosheet devices through the 1-nm-equivalent generation [4].

For an academic design group the transition to GAA raises three practical questions. First, how is the device represented in a commercial simulator so that circuit results are trustworthy? Second, how does the layout differ from a FinFET standard cell and how is it delivered as a foundry-readable GDSII stream? Third, can the full digital implementation flow, from RTL to GDSII, be exercised on a GAA library when the EDA tools run on shared or virtualised hardware, as is common in teaching laboratories? This paper answers all three with a single, small, fully documented design: a minimum-size CMOS inverter.

The inverter is chosen deliberately. It is the smallest complete CMOS cell, its static and dynamic figures of merit are the ones every library characterisation report starts with, and every step of the flow (device model, schematic, layout, DRC/LVS, GDSII stream-out, synthesis, placement, routing, extraction, final stream-out) is exercised without the noise of a larger design. The contributions are:

  • A calibrated GAA nanosheet model set for Cadence Spectre based on the BSIM-CMG multi-gate model [5], with a generic 3-nm-class geometry (Table I), and a dependency-free reference compact model that reproduces the same metrics for cross-checking.
  • A GAA inverter standard cell at a 6-track, 168-nm height with two 48-nm gate pitches, drawn to a published layer map and delivered as a Calma GDSII stream that reads back cleanly in an independent parser.
  • A complete RTL-to-GDSII implementation of the three RTL designs with library views characterised from the cells (Liberty, LEF), synthesis, obstruction-aware placement and routing, DEF and GDSII stream-out, and post-route DRC, LVS, extraction and timing, all released as scripts.
  • Parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation of every cell: device-level gate-to-epi coupling, contact and via resistance and metal RC extracted from the GDSII into SPEF and back-annotated, showing that the three-sheet gate parasitics, not the wiring, set the post-layout delay.
  • Physical verification of every delivered GDSII with a 26-rule GAA3 design-rule deck and a layout-versus-schematic extraction, both released as scripts; the first DRC pass exposed 79 violations that were corrected, and all cells are DRC-clean and LVS-matched.
  • A NAND2 standard cell that exploits the nanosheet width freedom by swapping the N and P band widths to balance the series stack in the minimum 3-pitch footprint, with its GDSII, testbench and a FinFET comparison.
  • A 6T SRAM bitcell in the thin-cell topology whose cell and pull-up ratios are set by sheet width (36 / 24 / 20 nm) in a 0.0207 µm² high-density footprint, with GDSII, testbench, and static noise margin, write and read analysis against a 1-1-1 FinFET cell.
  • A ring-oscillator study: an 11-stage FO3 ring built from the cell as a Spectre testbench, as synthesisable RTL with preserved stages, and as a hierarchical GDSII, characterised over supply voltage against the FinFET baseline.
  • A scripted RTL-to-GDSII flow (Xcelium, Genus, Innovus) that synthesises and physically implements the inverter on the GAA library and streams out the routed block, together with the VMware Workstation configuration used to host the tools.

Section II describes the device and its model. Section III details the virtual environment, the cell-level flow and the RTL-to-GDSII flow. Section IV presents the results, Section V discusses limitations, and Section VI concludes. All scripts are listed in the Appendix.

II.GAA Nanosheet Device and Compact Model

A.Device structure

Fig. 1 shows the cross-section of the device used in this work, cut along the gate; Fig. 2 gives the transistor-level schematics of the four circuits built from it and Fig. 3 the same schematics as captured in the Virtuoso editor. Three silicon nanosheets of thickness TNS = 5 nm are stacked with a 9-nm vertical spacing that is filled by the work-function metal gate; the gate therefore wraps each sheet completely. The NMOS sheet width is WNS,N = 30 nm and the PMOS sheet width is WNS,P = 45 nm, which is the GAA equivalent of the FinFET's fin-count ratio and sets the inverter's β ratio. The gate length is Lg = 14 nm, with a 0.9-nm equivalent oxide thickness. The effective electrical width of a stack of N sheets is the total wrapped perimeter,

Weff = N · 2 (WNS + TNS)(1)

which gives 210 nm for the NMOS and 300 nm for the PMOS stack in a footprint of only 30 nm and 45 nm respectively. This width-per-footprint advantage over a fin (whose perimeter is 2Hfin + Wfin for a much taller structure) is one of the two reasons GAA is adopted; the other is the sub-70-mV/dec subthreshold swing that the wrapped gate maintains at 14 nm [1], [3].

B.BSIM-CMG representation in Spectre

Cadence Spectre supports the Berkeley BSIM-CMG common multi-gate model natively [5]. A nanosheet stack is represented with the double-gate geometry mode (geomod=0) in which tfin is the sheet thickness, hfin the sheet width and nfin the number of sheets, so the model's effective width is exactly (1). Substrate coupling is disabled (bulkmod=0) because the stack sits on an isolated bottom dielectric. The remaining parameters (gate work function phig, mobility u0, saturation velocity vsat, series resistance rdsw, short-channel terms dvt0/dvt1/eta0) were set to reproduce the IRDS 3-nm-class targets in Table I. The two model cards are listed in the Appendix (Listing 3).

C.Reference compact model

Because BSIM-CMG is only available inside the licensed simulator, a small reference model was written so the electrical figures can be reproduced anywhere and used as an acceptance check on the Spectre run. It uses a unified weak-to-strong-inversion charge expression in the EKV style with a velocity-saturation exponent α and a DIBL-like output-conductance term:

ID = K · Vovα · g(VDS),  Vov = α n φt ln[1 + exp((VGS − Vth)/α n φt)](2)
g(VDS) = (VDS/VDSAT) [1 + (VDS/VDSAT)²]−1/2 (1 + λ VDS)(3)

where n = SS/(φt ln 10) reproduces the specified subthreshold swing exactly in weak inversion and K is fixed by the on-current target at VGS = VDS = VDD. Table I lists the calibration and the resulting device figures.

III.Design Methodology

A.Virtualised EDA environment

All Cadence tools were run in a Linux guest under VMware Workstation on a Windows host, the configuration typical of an academic VLSI laboratory where licences are served over the campus network. The guest is a Red Hat-family distribution from the Cadence support matrix with 4 virtual cores, 16 GB RAM and a 120-GB thin-provisioned disk; NAT networking reaches the FlexNet licence server through CDS_LIC_FILE, and a VMware shared folder maps the project repository into the guest so that scripts edited on the host are visible to the tools without copying. A snapshot taken after installation makes a broken flow recoverable in seconds. The environment variables and paths used are given in the project README and reproduced in Listing 8.

Two virtualisation effects were relevant to the flow. Spectre's multithreading benefits from pinning the guest to physical cores rather than hyper-threads, and Innovus's memory-mapped design database needs the guest's swap to be at least as large as its RAM to avoid silent aborts during routing. Neither affects results, only run time.

B.Cell design in Virtuoso and Spectre

The inverter schematic (Fig. 2(a) and Fig. 3, Listing 3 subcircuit) instantiates one PMOS and one NMOS nanosheet stack between VDD and VSS. The testbench applies a piecewise-linear input with a 12-ps 10–90 % slew and drives a fan-out-of-4 load of 1.28 fF (four times the 0.32-fF input capacitance of the cell itself); a 0.35-fF lumped parasitic on the output stands in for drain, contact and gate-fringe capacitance before extraction. Three analyses are run: a DC sweep for the voltage-transfer characteristic (VTC), a transient for delay and energy, and a two-point DC for static leakage. Spectre's export measurements extract VM, tpHL, tpLH, energy per cycle and static power directly, so the same numbers are produced by ADE and by the batch run.

C.Layout and GDSII generation

The physical cell follows the 6-track template of a 3-nm-class library: height 6 × 28 nm = 168 nm, width two contacted gate pitches (2 × 48 nm = 96 nm), with half of a dummy diffusion-break gate on each vertical edge so that abutting cells share it. Table II lists the layer map. The GAA-specific features are the two nanosheet bands (layer 2) whose heights are the sheet widths of Table I, a stack-count marker (layer 2, datatype 1) that documents the three sheets for the technology file, and a gate-cut marker (layer 3, datatype 1) which is left open over the active gate because the inverter's N and P gates are common. Source/drain trench contacts (layer 4) land on the sheet bands, the gate contact (layer 5) sits in the 24-nm N/P separation region, via-0 (layer 6) connects to metal-1 (layer 7) which carries the two 24-nm power rails straddling the cell boundary, the source straps, the vertical output bar joining the two drains and the input landing pad. Pins are marked as datatype 1 and named with datatype 2 texts, which is the convention Innovus reads back from the merged cell GDS.

The layout was built in Virtuoso Layout XL and, in parallel, generated by the Python script of Listing 6, which contains a complete Calma GDSII stream writer (HEADER, BGNLIB, UNITS, BGNSTR, BOUNDARY, TEXT, SREF and the excess-64 real encoding) in about 100 lines and no third-party dependency. Having a second, independent producer of the same polygons served two purposes: it made the layer map an executable document, and it let the GDSII be regenerated and inspected in the host operating system where Virtuoso is not installed. Stream-out from Virtuoso uses strmout or the SKILL xstOut call of Listing 7 with the same layer map; stream-in of the script-generated file into Virtuoso produces an identical layout cellview, which was verified by XOR in the layout editor.

D.RTL-to-GDSII flow

Fig. 5 shows the digital implementation flow. The RTL (Listing 1) is a single continuous assignment; the value of running it through the flow is that every tool touches the GAA library. Genus reads the Liberty, LEF and RTL, elaborates, applies the constraints of Listing 2 (a 200-ps virtual clock, FO4 output load, 15-ps maximum transition) and maps onto the GAA3 library, where it selects INV_GAA_X1 (Listing 4). Innovus (Listing 5) imports the mapped netlist under a three-corner multi-mode multi-corner setup (typical, slow 0.63 V/125 °C, fast 0.77 V/−40 °C), floorplans a single 168-nm row at 60 % utilisation, routes the metal-1 follow-pin rails, places and optimises, routes with NanoRoute up to metal-4, adds filler cells, runs DRC and connectivity checks, extracts parasitics to SPEF, performs post-route timing and power analysis, and finally streams the routed block to GDSII with streamOut, merging the standard-cell GDS so the delivered file is complete down to the nanosheet layer.

IV.Results

Provenance. The figures and numbers in this section were produced by the reference compact model of Section II-C (spectre/ref_model.py), calibrated to the Table I targets. They are the acceptance values against which the Spectre/BSIM-CMG run of Listing 3 and the post-layout Innovus reports are compared in the VMware guest; the Spectre and Innovus report values should replace them in the final version of the manuscript.

A.Device characteristics

Fig. 6 shows the transfer characteristics of the two stacks. The subthreshold slopes are 68 mV/dec (NMOS) and 70 mV/dec (PMOS) by construction, the on-currents are 210 µA and 225 µA, and the resulting ION/IOFF ratios of 75 × 10³ and 105 × 10³ are consistent with published 3-nm GAA data at a standard threshold flavour [3]. The near-balance of N and P on-current at a 30/45-nm sheet-width ratio is the direct consequence of (1): the PMOS's 1.43 × wider sheets compensate its 0.75 × lower current density, which is exactly the design freedom fin quantisation removes.

B.Static transfer characteristic

Fig. 7 shows the VTC and its slope. The switching threshold VM = 350 mV sits at 50 % of VDD, confirming the β-ratio choice. The maximum small-signal gain of 28 is high for a 14-nm device and reflects the low output conductance of the wrapped gate; it produces a steep transition with unity-gain points at VIL = 295 mV and VIH = 395 mV. Output levels are VOH = 661 mV and VOL = 40 mV, so the noise margins are NML = 255 mV and NMH = 266 mV, each above 36 % of the supply.

C.Transient response, delay and energy

Fig. 8 shows the response to the 12-ps-slew input step for the intrinsic (FO1) and FO4 loads, and Fig. 9 collects the corresponding viewer displays for all four circuits with the markers used to extract the figures of merit. Table III summarises the timing and energy figures. The FO4 propagation delay of 5.77 ps and the near-equal tpHL/tpLH again confirm the drive balance. The energy of 0.84 fJ per full cycle at FO4 corresponds to 0.84 µW at 1 GHz with 100 % activity, while the static power is 1.74 nW, a dynamic-to-static ratio of about 484 at 1 GHz.

The delivered stream file was read back with an independent parser (gdstk 1.0) and by Virtuoso stream-in. Both report one structure, INV_GAA_X1, in library GAA3_INV_LIB with a 1-nm database unit, 32 boundary elements on the 11 layer/datatype pairs of Table IV, four text elements (A, Y, VDD, VSS) on layer 7:2, and a bounding box of (−7, −12) to (103, 180) nm, i.e. the 96 × 168-nm cell plus the half dummy gates and half rails that extend past the placement boundary by design. The Innovus block-level stream is the same cell merged with the row's filler cells, power rails and the two metal-2 pins.

E.Comparison with a FinFET inverter

To quantify what the change of device brings, the same reference model, testbench and cell template were re-run with a 5-nm-class FinFET calibration: an 18-nm gate, 50-nm-tall and 6-nm-wide fins at a 27-nm fin pitch, two fins per device in a 6-track 180-nm cell at a 54-nm contacted gate pitch, with subthreshold swings of 72/74 mV/dec and the higher drain-induced barrier lowering of a tri-gate channel [2], [4], [6]. Table V sets the two side by side. Because a fin adds drive only in whole-fin steps, the FinFET PMOS is limited to the same two fins as the NMOS and so delivers only 148 µA against 191 µA, which shows up as a 1.24-ps rise/fall skew and a 335-mV switching threshold; the GAA cell tunes the P sheet to 45 nm and balances the edges to within 0.01 ps. The three wrapped 30-nm sheets fit a 210-nm effective width into a 30-nm footprint, where two fins need 54 nm of pitch for 212 nm. The result is a 16 % lower FO4 delay and a 17 % smaller cell for essentially the same energy per cycle, since the switched capacitance is set by the load and the parasitics rather than by the channel.

F.Ring oscillator

A ring oscillator (RO) is the standard vehicle for reporting a technology's switching speed because it removes the arbitrary stimulus slew of a single-inverter measurement: each stage is driven by the natural edge of the previous one. An 11-stage RO was built from INV_GAA_X1 in the fan-out-of-3 configuration used for library characterisation, in which every node drives the next stage plus two dummy inverters. The Spectre testbench (Listing 11) kick-starts the loop with an initial condition and sweeps VDD from 0.5 to 0.8 V; the RTL of Listing 12 keeps the eleven stages through synthesis with preserve attributes so Genus and Innovus can implement the same ring, and Listing 13 generates the hierarchical RO GDSII of Fig. 11 from eleven abutted inverter cells wired on metal-2. The reference model reproduces the RO by integrating the eleven node voltages with each node loaded by 3 Cin + Cpar = 1.31 fF.

Fig. 10 shows the steady-state waveforms and the supply dependence. At 0.7 V the GAA ring oscillates at 12.1 GHz, a stage delay of 3.77 ps, drawing 86 µW, i.e. 652 aJ per stage per cycle; the FinFET ring built the same way runs at 9.1 GHz (4.99 ps per stage). The stage delay is well below the step-driven FO4 delay of Table III because the ring's own edges are much faster than the 12-ps stimulus used there. Frequency scales almost linearly with supply over the sweep, the signature of a velocity-saturated device, and the GAA advantage of 32 % at nominal supply widens to -4 % at 0.5 V where its lower threshold and steeper swing matter most. The energy per stage follows C VDD², so the energy-delay product favours the GAA ring by 23 % at 0.7 V.

G.Two-input NAND gate

The NAND2 is the first cell in which the GAA width freedom changes a design decision rather than a number. Its pull-down is two NMOS in series and its pull-up two PMOS in parallel, so with the inverter's 30-nm N / 45-nm P bands the worst-case pull-down (one series stack) would be roughly half the pull-up (one PMOS). In a FinFET library this is corrected by adding a fin to each NMOS, which adds a whole fin pitch to the cell; a nanosheet cell simply swaps the two band widths. NAND2_GAA_X1 (Fig. 12) therefore uses 45-nm sheets for the series NMOS and 30-nm sheets for the parallel PMOS, in the same 6-track template and the minimum three gate pitches (144 nm). The internal stack node X is a contact-only diffusion, the output is collected on metal-2 through via-1 from the shared PMOS drain and the outer NMOS drain, and the two gate contacts sit in a 35-nm N/P gap on the input track. Listing 15 is the Spectre testbench with width-swapped BSIM-CMG cards, Listing 16 the RTL that Genus maps onto the cell, and Listing 17 the GDSII generator.

Fig. 13 shows the three transfer curves and the two timing arcs. With the swapped bands the series stack delivers 165 µA against 157 µA for a single PMOS, a ratio of 1.05, so the tied-input switching threshold of 375 mV is near mid-supply and the two single-input arcs are within 0.15 ps of each other. The FinFET cell, held at two fins per device, has a pull-down/pull-up ratio of 0.69 and a 8.66-ps worst-case delay against 7.60 ps, while occupying 21 % more area. The B-input high-to-low arc is the slower of the two falling arcs in both technologies: its transistor is the outer device of the stack, so its transition must also discharge the internal node before the output starts to fall. The leakage rows show the stack effect: with both inputs low the two off NMOS in series leak 2.9 × less than a single off device because the internal node settles a few tens of millivolts above ground, which gives the top device a negative gate-source voltage and the bottom device a smaller drain bias, an effect the reference model captures through the internal-node DC solution and BSIM-CMG through its full subthreshold formulation.

H.Six-transistor SRAM bitcell

SRAM is where the nanosheet's continuous width matters most, because a bitcell's stability and writability are set by two ratios that a FinFET high-density cell cannot tune: the cell ratio β = IPD/IPG that limits the read disturb, and the pull-up ratio γ = IPG/IPU that sets the write trip point. A 1-fin-per-device FinFET cell has β = 1 by construction and can only reach β = 2 by adding a whole fin to the pull-down, which is the high-performance cell with roughly a third more area. The GAA bitcell of Fig. 14, SRAM6T_GAA_HD, keeps the thin-cell topology [12] at two gate pitches of height (96 nm) and 216 nm of width (0.0207 µm², in line with the 0.020–0.021 µm² high-density cells reported at 3 nm [3], [4]) and sets the ratios by sheet width alone: the NMOS stripe is jogged so the pull-down uses 36-nm sheets and the access transistor 24-nm sheets, and the pull-up uses 20-nm sheets, chosen so that the write trip point matches the FinFET cell. The two inverters are cross-coupled through butted contacts that join the end of each gate row to the opposite storage node's PMOS drain; bit lines, supply and ground run vertically on metal-2 and the word line horizontally on metal-3. Listing 19 is the Spectre testbench (butterfly curves with the loop broken by a controlled source, write sweep, read current, leakage and a supply sweep) and Listing 20 the GDSII generator; Listing 21 is the reference analysis, which solves each storage node by bisection and extracts the static noise margin as the largest square that fits between a transfer curve and its mirror.

Table VIII and Fig. 15 give the results. The hold static noise margin, set by the two inverter transfer curves alone, is within 5 % of the FinFET cell's, since the GAA pull-up is deliberately its weakest device; the read margin is where the sizing pays: the GAA cell's β = 1.41 holds the '0' node to 135 mV during a read against 169 mV for the β = 1 FinFET cell, which lifts the read SNM from 94 mV to 105 mV. On the write side the pull-up width sets γ = 1.55, which puts the write trip voltage at 293 mV against 294 mV for the FinFET cell: the read-margin gain is obtained at unchanged writability, and a wider pull-up would trade it back for hold margin. The read current, which sets the bit-line discharge time and therefore the access time, is 112.1 µA against 51.4 µA. Fig. 15 (right) shows that the read margin scales with supply almost as steadily as the hold margin down to 0.4 V, which is the property that lets GAA SRAM lower its minimum operating voltage. The cost of the wider pull-down is visible in the leakage row; a production cell would use a high-threshold flavour of the same devices, which the SVT calibration of Table I does not represent.

I.Physical verification: DRC and LVS

Every GDSII delivered with this paper was checked against the GAA3 rule deck and against its schematic before release. The deck (Listing 26) has 26 rules of five kinds: minimum width, same-layer spacing measured as the Euclidean gap, spacing between layers, enclosure of a via or a sheet band by the layer above it, and required overlap of a contact with its target. Two rules encode nanosheet-specific structure: the sheet-band spacing rule is set to the 16-nm gap of a single diffusion break so that abutted cells sharing a dummy gate are legal, and the SDC-to-gate spacing rule exempts a trench contact that carries a gate contact, which is the butted contact that cross-couples the SRAM cell. The checker evaluates each rule with polygon booleans (erosion and dilation for width and spacing, dilation and difference for enclosure) on the flattened cell; Pegasus in the VMware guest runs the same rule names for sign-off. LVS (Listing 27) extracts the netlist from the same polygons: the diffusion segments are the sheet bands minus the gates, every gate-band intersection is a transistor whose type comes from the well, whose width is the band extent along the gate and whose source and drain are the two adjacent segments; contacts, vias and metals are joined by overlap, supplies are virtually connected by name, and the port names come from the text labels. The extracted graph is compared with the Spectre subcircuit by colour refinement over device type, sheet width and terminal roles, so unnamed internal nets such as the NAND2 stack node or the eleven ring nodes are matched by structure.

Table IX shows why the check matters. The first DRC pass on the layouts as drawn found 79 violations: an input pad only 4 nm from the supply straps and 1 nm from the output bar in the inverter, which the ring oscillator replicated twenty-two times; a gate via mis-centred on its contact in the NAND2; and, in the SRAM cell, pads that enclosed their vias by less than 3 nm, bit-line stubs 11 nm from the word-line pickups and the P-type sheet bands reaching the edge of the well. All were corrected in the generators (the inverter's output contact moved 3 nm to the right and its supply straps stopped 12 nm clear of the pad; the SRAM metal-2 tracks re-spaced at the 28-nm pitch with the word-line pickups on the shared cell edges), and the final pass is clean on all four cells. Table X summarises the LVS comparison: every cell matches its schematic in ports, nets and instances, including the 22 devices and 13 nets of the flattened ring. Fig. 16 and Fig. 17 show the results as the Pegasus results viewers present them.

J.Parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation

The last step of the cell-level flow is to replace the lumped parasitic estimates of the pre-layout testbenches with values extracted from the drawn geometry. In the guest this is Quantus QRC run on the LVS database with the command file of Listing 33, which writes a SPEF that ADE back-annotates onto the av_extracted view; here the reference extractor of Listing 34 performs the same three computations on the GDSII and writes the same SPEF (Listing 35). At device level it charges each transistor with a gate-to-source and a gate-to-drain parasitic capacitance of 0.25 aF per nanometre of effective width, the inner-spacer and epitaxy capacitance of a three-sheet stack [1], [3], which dominates every other term. At contact level it adds the trench-contact resistance ρc/A with ρc = 10−9 Ω cm² and fixed via resistances of 45, 35 and 30 Ω. At interconnect level it uses the layer heights of the GAA3 stack with a k = 2.9 dielectric for area, fringe and lateral coupling capacitance (ε t/gap between facing edges), overlap capacitance between adjacent layers and a sheet resistance of 22, 18 and 15 Ω/□ for metal-1 to metal-3. Supplies are decoupled ground nets, so their couplings count as ground capacitance, and the schematic's intrinsic gate capacitance CoxWeffLg stays in the device model.

Table XI lists the extracted nets of the four cells and Fig. 18 shows the extraction summaries as Quantus presents them. The inverter's input net carries 131 aF of parasitic capacitance to ground and 129 aF of coupling to the output, so its post-layout input capacitance is 0.66 fF against the 0.32 fF assumed pre-layout: the placeholder was optimistic on the gate side. The output net, by contrast, carries only 0.021 fF of contact and metal capacitance plus the same coupling, against the 0.35 fF lumped pre-layout, and 253 Ω of series resistance between the drains and the output pin. Post-layout simulation (Listing 36) applies these values exactly: the gate-drain coupling of the driver enters the output node through d(Vin − Vout)/dt, the same coupling on each of the four loads is doubled for the Miller effect, and half the extracted net resistance separates the driver from its load. Table XII and Fig. 19 give the results. The inverter's FO4 delay rises from 5.77 ps to 8.42 ps (+46 %) and its energy per cycle from 0.84 to 1.43 fJ, almost entirely because the four loads now present 2.65 fF instead of 1.28 fF. The ring oscillator slows from 12.1 to 7.2 GHz (6.33 ps per stage) with the metal-2 stubs, the feedback line and the two dummy loads per node extracted, and the NAND2 worst-case arc moves from 7.60 to 9.39 ps. For the bitcell the extraction gives 68 aF of bit-line capacitance and 216 aF of word-line capacitance per cell with 225 Ω of word-line metal per cell, from which a 256-cell bit line develops the 100-mV sense margin in 15.5 ps at the read current of Table VIII and a 64-cell word-line segment has an Elmore delay of 99.5 ps.

Two conclusions follow for the flow. First, the pre-layout figures of Tables III, VI and VII should be read as the lower bound they are: the placeholder input capacitance underestimated the gate parasitics of a three-sheet stack by 2.1 ×, and every delay in this paper that is quoted for design comparison should be the post-layout one. Second, the wiring itself is not the problem at this cell size: the metal-1 and metal-2 parasitics are below 10 aF per net and the extracted resistances add less than 2 % to the delay; the device-level gate-to-epi capacitance is where a nanosheet library's speed is decided, which is why sheet count and spacer engineering matter more than the metal stack for these cells.

K.RTL-to-GDSII implementation results

The digital flow of Section III-D was exercised on the three RTL designs (the inverter, the NAND2 and the enabled ring oscillator of Listings 1, 16 and 12) with the GAA3 library views that the cell-level work produces. Characterising INV_GAA_X1 and NAND2_GAA_X1 with the post-layout model over three input slews and four loads gives the Liberty file of Listing 37 (non-linear delay tables for delay and output transition, pin capacitance from extraction, leakage and switching energy); the layouts give the technology and cell LEF of Listing 38 (site, routing layers, pin ports and the metal-2 obstruction of the NAND2). The Genus step (Listing 39) reads the RTL, elaborates vectors and generate loops, maps onto the two cells (NOT to INV, NAND to NAND2, AND to NAND2 plus INV) and writes the mapped netlist, the constraints and the gate, timing and power reports; Genus cuts the ring's combinational loop at the feedback input of the enable gate, so the reported path runs from en through the NAND2 and the twelve inverters to out. The Innovus step (Listing 40) floorplans one 168-nm row at 60 % utilisation, places the cells in chain order with fillers in the gaps, assigns the I/O pins to metal-2 tracks on the die edges, routes every net on a metal-2 track chosen so that horizontal segments, the vertical jogs to the pins and the cells' metal-2 obstructions keep the 12-nm spacing, and streams out DEF and GDSII with the cell references and the routing. The routed GDSII then goes back through the checks of Sections IV-I and IV-J: DRC against the GAA3 deck, LVS against the mapped netlist, extraction to SPEF and post-route timing with the extracted wire capacitance added to the Liberty pin loads.

Table XIII summarises synthesis and Table XIV the physical implementation; Fig. 20 shows the routed designs as the Innovus main window presents them and Fig. 21 the Genus and Innovus report windows. The inverter and NAND2 designs are single cells with two fillers each; the ring is 13 cells (twelve inverters and the enable NAND2) in a 2160 × 168 nm core, 14 nets routed on two metal-2 tracks with 3903 nm of wire and 26 vias, and its en-to-out path of 47.2 ps at synthesis becomes 49.2 ps after routing and extraction, well inside the 200-ps virtual clock. All three routed blocks are DRC-clean and LVS-matched to their netlists. The first routing pass was not: the router initially ignored the NAND2's cell-internal metal-2, ran the b net over it and shorted it to y, which the post-route LVS caught as a missing port and the DRC as a metal-2 spacing error; the obstruction-aware track selection and the placement rule that puts obstructed cells at the row end are the corrections. The same flow scripts drive the sign-off tools in the guest (Listings 4, 5 and 12b); the reference implementation exists so that every deliverable of the flow, from the Liberty tables to the routed GDSII, can be regenerated and checked outside the licensed environment.

V.Discussion

Position against the roadmap. The geometry of Table I matches the IRDS 2023 "3-nm" logic node (14–16-nm gate length, 45–48-nm contacted gate pitch, 24–28-nm minimum metal pitch, 0.7-V supply) [4], and the FO4 delay and energy of Table III are in the range reported for early GAA nanosheet ring oscillators and inverters [1], [3]. The 6-track cell height of 168 nm is at the roadmap value; the 96-nm width is the minimum for a single-gate cell with shared diffusion breaks.

What GAA changes in the cell. Table V makes the trade explicit for the inverter, Table VII for the NAND2, where the sheet-width swap replaces a fin-count change, and Table VIII for the SRAM bitcell, where three different sheet widths set the cell and pull-up ratios that a one-fin cell cannot adjust. Compared with a FinFET inverter at the same pitch, the layout has no fin grid: drive is set by the height of the nanosheet band, which the layout engineer can choose per device within the design-rule window, and the N/P sheet-width ratio replaces the fin-count ratio. The stack-count marker and the gate-cut layer are new; the rest of the metallisation is unchanged, which is why the RTL-to-GDSII flow needed no modification beyond pointing at the GAA library.

Limitations. The rule set is generic; a foundry 3-nm GAA PDK has different layer numbering, an additional buried power rail or backside power option, and considerably tighter and more numerous rules, so the layout here should be treated as a topology, not as tape-out ready; the DRC-clean and LVS-matched status of Section IV-I holds for the GAA3 deck, not for a foundry deck, and the extracted parasitics of Section IV-J use a generic technology table whose device-level coefficient sets the post-layout delay almost by itself. The results section reports reference-model values that must be replaced by the Spectre/BSIM-CMG and post-layout Innovus figures once the flow is executed in the licensed environment; the model was calibrated to the same targets so the two are expected to agree within the calibration tolerance, and Section IV-J shows what extraction changes: the gate-side parasitics were underestimated and the post-layout delays are the ones to quote. The ring-oscillator frequencies are optimistic for the same reason, since the model carries no Miller or gate-overlap capacitance and no interconnect load; the BSIM-CMG cards include cgso/cgdo and the Innovus SPEF adds the wiring, so the Spectre and post-layout RO frequencies will be lower. Variability (sheet-thickness and work-function variation) and self-heating in the stacked, dielectrically isolated channel were not analysed and are natural next steps.

Reproducibility. Every script referenced in this paper is listed in the Appendix and released in the project repository under vlsi/gaa_inverter/. The GDSII files, the SVG renderings of their polygons, the schematics of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 and the reference-model results are regenerated by Python commands with no dependencies beyond the standard library; PNG renderings of every schematic and layout are kept under docs/figures/.

VI.Conclusion

A gate-all-around nanosheet CMOS inverter was designed, laid out and carried through a complete Cadence RTL-to-GDSII flow inside a VMware Workstation guest. The device was represented with BSIM-CMG in Spectre, the cell was drawn to a documented 3-nm-class layer map and delivered as a verified GDSII stream, and Genus and Innovus synthesised and physically implemented the cell to a second, block-level GDSII. At 0.7 V the inverter shows a 350-mV switching threshold, a gain of 28, noise margins above 250 mV, a 5.77-ps FO4 delay and 0.84 fJ per cycle in 0.0161 µm², and an 11-stage FO3 ring oscillator built from it runs at 12.1 GHz, 32 % faster than the FinFET ring. The NAND2 cell shows the design consequence of continuous width tuning: swapping the sheet widths of the two bands balances the series stack without the extra fin pitch a FinFET cell needs, and the 6T bitcell turns the same freedom into a 12 % higher read margin at the same write trip point and equal area. Because every artefact, from the model card to the stream writer, is scripted and released, the work serves as a template for research groups moving to GAA technology on virtualised EDA infrastructure, and as the cell-level foundation for larger GAA standard-cell libraries and memory arrays.

The listings below are the exact files released with the paper. Paths are relative to vlsi/gaa_inverter/.

Listing 1. RTL of the inverter (Verilog-2005) · rtl/inverter.v
// inverter.v -- RTL for the GAA nanosheet inverter demonstrator.
// Synthesised by Cadence Genus onto the GAA3 standard-cell library (INV_GAA_X1).
`timescale 1ps/1fs
module inverter (
    input  wire a,   // input
    output wire y    // y = ~a
);
    assign y = ~a;
endmodule
Listing 2. Timing constraints · genus/constraints.sdc
# constraints.sdc -- timing constraints for the inverter (GAA3 library, 0.7 V, 25 C)
set_units -time ps -capacitance fF
create_clock -name vclk -period 200 ;# virtual clock, 5 GHz budget
set_input_delay  -clock vclk 20 [get_ports a]
set_output_delay -clock vclk 20 [get_ports y]
set_driving_cell -lib_cell INV_GAA_X1 [get_ports a]
set_load 1.28 [get_ports y]          ;# FO4 load: 4 x 0.32 fF INV_GAA_X1 input cap
set_max_transition 15 [current_design]
Listing 3. Spectre testbench with BSIM-CMG nanosheet model cards · spectre/gaa_inv_tb.scs
// gaa_inv_tb.scs -- Spectre testbench: GAA nanosheet inverter, BSIM-CMG (multi-gate) models
// Run: spectre gaa_inv_tb.scs +log spectre.log  (Virtuoso ADE: import as netlist)
simulator lang=spectre
global 0 vdd!

// ---- BSIM-CMG nanosheet model cards (generic 3-nm-class calibration) --------
// GEOMOD=0 (double-gate) with NFIN = number of sheets and effective width via
// TFIN (sheet thickness) & HFIN (sheet width): W_eff = NFIN * 2 * (HFIN + TFIN)
model nsheet_n bsimcmg type=n  version=110.0 bulkmod=0 geomod=0 devtype=1 \
      l=14e-9 tfin=5e-9 hfin=30e-9 nfin=3 eot=0.9e-9 toxp=1.2e-9 \
      phig=4.36 nbody=1e22 u0=0.030 vsat=1.2e5 rdsw=90 \
      dvt0=1.2 dvt1=0.45 eta0=0.06 cit=1e-4 cgso=1.2e-10 cgdo=1.2e-10
model nsheet_p bsimcmg type=p  version=110.0 bulkmod=0 geomod=0 devtype=0 \
      l=14e-9 tfin=5e-9 hfin=45e-9 nfin=3 eot=0.9e-9 toxp=1.2e-9 \
      phig=4.86 nbody=1e22 u0=0.022 vsat=1.0e5 rdsw=110 \
      dvt0=1.2 dvt1=0.45 eta0=0.07 cit=1e-4 cgso=1.3e-10 cgdo=1.3e-10

// ---- inverter subcircuit (matches INV_GAA_X1 layout) --------------------------
subckt INV_GAA_X1 (A Y VDD VSS)
    MP (Y A VDD VDD) nsheet_p
    MN (Y A VSS VSS) nsheet_n
    CparY (Y VSS) capacitor c=0.35f          // drain/contact parasitics (pre-extraction)
ends INV_GAA_X1

// ---- stimulus -----------------------------------------------------------------
parameters vsup=0.70 tslew=12p cload=1.28f  // cload = FO4 (4 x 0.32 fF)
Vdd (vdd! 0) vsource dc=vsup
Vin (in 0)   vsource type=pwl wave=[0 0 10p 0 25p vsup 45p vsup 60p 0 80p 0]
X1  (in out vdd! 0) INV_GAA_X1
CL  (out 0) capacitor c=cload

// ---- analyses -----------------------------------------------------------------
dcvtc  dc dev=Vin param=dc start=0 stop=vsup step=5m
tran   tran stop=80p step=2f errpreset=conservative
leak   dc dev=Vin param=dc values=[0 vsup]

// ---- measurements (Spectre .measure equivalents via 'export'/MDL) -----------
export vm    = value( v(out), v(in) == v(out) )
export tpHL  = cross(sig=v(out) dir='fall n=1 thresh=vsup/2) - cross(sig=v(in) dir='rise n=1 thresh=vsup/2)
export tpLH  = cross(sig=v(out) dir='rise n=1 thresh=vsup/2) - cross(sig=v(in) dir='fall n=1 thresh=vsup/2)
export Ecyc  = integ(-i(Vdd)*vsup, from=0, to=80p)
export Pstat = -i(Vdd) * vsup

saveOptions options save=allpub
Listing 4. Genus synthesis script · genus/synth.tcl
# synth.tcl -- Cadence Genus synthesis script (RTL -> mapped netlist) for the GAA3 library
# Invoke in the VMware guest:  genus -files synth.tcl -log logs/genus
set DESIGN inverter
set LIB_DIR  $env(GAA3_LIB)                       ;# e.g. /opt/pdk/gaa3/lib
set_db init_lib_search_path  [list $LIB_DIR/liberty $LIB_DIR/lef]
set_db init_hdl_search_path  ../rtl
set_db library    [list gaa3_stdcells_tt_0p70v_25c.lib]
set_db lef_library [list gaa3_tech.lef gaa3_stdcells.lef]
set_db information_level 7
set_db hdl_error_on_blackbox true
set_db syn_generic_effort high
set_db syn_map_effort     high
set_db syn_opt_effort     high

read_hdl -sv ${DESIGN}.v
elaborate $DESIGN
check_design -unresolved
read_sdc constraints.sdc

syn_generic
syn_map
syn_opt

file mkdir out reports
write_hdl        > out/${DESIGN}_netlist.v
write_sdc        > out/${DESIGN}.sdc
write_sdf -edges check_edge -setuphold split -recrem split > out/${DESIGN}.sdf
write_design -innovus -base_name out/${DESIGN}
report_timing -nworst 5 > reports/timing.rpt
report_area           > reports/area.rpt
report_power          > reports/power.rpt
report_gates          > reports/gates.rpt
puts "Genus: mapped $DESIGN onto [get_db [get_db insts] .base_cell.name]"
exit

# pnr.tcl -- Cadence Innovus place-and-route script: mapped netlist -> GDSII
# Invoke:  innovus -init pnr.tcl -log logs/innovus
set DESIGN inverter
set LIB_DIR $env(GAA3_LIB)

# ---- 1. design import ---------------------------------------------------
set init_verilog        ../genus/out/${DESIGN}_netlist.v
set init_top_cell       $DESIGN
set init_lef_file       [list $LIB_DIR/lef/gaa3_tech.lef $LIB_DIR/lef/gaa3_stdcells.lef]
set init_mmmc_file      mmmc.tcl
set init_pwr_net        VDD
set init_gnd_net        VSS
init_design

# ---- 2. floorplan: 6-track cell (168 nm) row, ~60 % utilisation -----------
floorPlan -site gaa3_core -r 1.0 0.60 0.096 0.168 0.096 0.168
globalNetConnect VDD -type pgpin -pin VDD -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type pgpin -pin VSS -inst * -verbose
# follow-pin power rails on M1 (24 nm) straddling the row boundaries
sroute -connect {corePin} -layerChangeRange {M1 M1} -nets {VDD VSS} \
       -corePinTarget {none} -allowJogging 1 -allowLayerChange 0

# ---- 3. placement -------------------------------------------------------------
setPlaceMode -place_global_place_io_pins true
place_opt_design
setPinAssignMode -pinEditInBatch true
editPin -pin a -layer M2 -side Left  -assign 0.000 0.084
editPin -pin y -layer M2 -side Right -assign 0.192 0.084
setPinAssignMode -pinEditInBatch false

# ---- 4. clock (none) / timing-driven optimisation --------------------------
optDesign -preCTS

# ---- 5. routing -----------------------------------------------------------------
setNanoRouteMode -routeWithTimingDriven true -routeWithSiDriven true \
                 -routeTopRoutingLayer 4 -routeBottomRoutingLayer 1
routeDesign
optDesign -postRoute -setup -hold

# ---- 6. fill, verification, extraction -------------------------------------------
addFiller -cell FILL_GAA_X1 -prefix FILL
verify_drc -report reports/drc.rpt
verifyConnectivity -type all -report reports/connectivity.rpt
extractRC
rcOut -spef out/${DESIGN}.spef
timeDesign -postRoute -outDir reports/timing_postroute
report_power -outfile reports/power_postroute.rpt

# ---- 7. deliverables ---------------------------------------------------------------
saveNetlist out/${DESIGN}_pnr.v -includePowerGround
write_sdf   out/${DESIGN}_pnr.sdf
defOut -floorplan -netlist -routing out/${DESIGN}.def
saveDesign  out/${DESIGN}.enc

# ---- 8. GDSII stream-out (Calma GDSII, 1 nm database unit) -------------------------
streamOut out/${DESIGN}.gds \
    -mapFile     ../layout/gaa3.layermap \
    -libName     GAA3_INV_LIB \
    -structureName $DESIGN \
    -merge       [list $LIB_DIR/gds/gaa3_stdcells.gds] \
    -units       1000 \
    -mode        ALL \
    -stripes     1 \
    -uniquifyCellNames
puts "Innovus: streamed out/${DESIGN}.gds"
exit

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
gen_gaa_inverter_gds.py
-----------------------
Generates the GDSII stream file of a gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet CMOS
inverter standard cell (INV_GAA_X1) with a dependency-free GDSII writer,
plus an SVG rendering of the same polygons and a JSON dump for documentation.

The geometry follows a generic 3-nm-class nanosheet design-rule set
(contacted gate pitch 48 nm, Lg 14 nm, 3 stacked sheets, 6-track cell,
M1 pitch 28 nm). Layer numbers follow the tech-file `gaa3.layermap`
shipped next to this script and used by the Innovus stream-out step.

Usage:
    python3 gen_gaa_inverter_gds.py            # writes gaa_inverter.gds, .svg, .json

The output can be read by Cadence Virtuoso (File > Import > Stream),
KLayout, or gdstk.  Database unit = 1 nm, user unit = 1 um.
"""
import json
import math
import struct
import time

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Minimal GDSII stream writer (Calma GDSII Stream Format, release 6)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
HEADER, BGNLIB, LIBNAME, UNITS, ENDLIB, BGNSTR, STRNAME, ENDSTR = (
    0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07)
BOUNDARY, PATH, SREF, TEXT, LAYER, DATATYPE, XY, ENDEL = (
    0x08, 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0C, 0x0D, 0x0E, 0x10, 0x11)
SNAME, TEXTTYPE, PRESENTATION, STRING, MAG, STRANS, ANGLE = 0x12, 0x16, 0x17, 0x19, 0x1B, 0x1A, 0x1C
WIDTH = 0x0F

DT_NONE, DT_BITARRAY, DT_INT2, DT_INT4, DT_REAL8, DT_ASCII = 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6


def _real8(value: float) -> bytes:
    """Encode a float as GDSII 8-byte excess-64 base-16 real."""
    if value == 0.0:
        return b"\x00" * 8
    sign = 0
    if value < 0:
        sign = 0x80
        value = -value
    exponent = 0
    while value >= 1.0:
        value /= 16.0
        exponent += 1
    while value < 1.0 / 16.0:
        value *= 16.0
        exponent -= 1
    mantissa = int(round(value * (1 << 56)))
    if mantissa >= (1 << 56):          # rounding overflow guard
        mantissa >>= 4
        exponent += 1
    return bytes([sign | (exponent + 64)]) + mantissa.to_bytes(7, "big")


def _record(rtype: int, dtype: int, payload: bytes = b"") -> bytes:
    length = 4 + len(payload)
    return struct.pack(">HBB", length, rtype, dtype) + payload


def _ascii(rtype: int, text: str) -> bytes:
    data = text.encode("ascii")
    if len(data) % 2:
        data += b"\x00"
    return _record(rtype, DT_ASCII, data)


def _int2(rtype: int, *values: int) -> bytes:
    return _record(rtype, DT_INT2, struct.pack(">%dh" % len(values), *values))


def _timestamp() -> bytes:
    t = time.localtime()
    stamp = (t.tm_year, t.tm_mon, t.tm_mday, t.tm_hour, t.tm_min, t.tm_sec)
    return struct.pack(">12h", *(stamp + stamp))


class GdsLibrary:
    def __init__(self, name: str, user_unit=1e-6, db_unit=1e-9):
        self.name = name
        self.user_unit = user_unit
        self.db_unit = db_unit
        self.cells = []

    def write(self, path: str) -> None:
        out = bytearray()
        out += _int2(HEADER, 600)
        out += _record(BGNLIB, DT_INT2, _timestamp())
        out += _ascii(LIBNAME, self.name)
        out += _record(UNITS, DT_REAL8,
                       _real8(self.db_unit / self.user_unit) + _real8(self.db_unit))
        for cell in self.cells:
            out += cell.to_bytes()
        out += _record(ENDLIB, DT_NONE)
        with open(path, "wb") as fh:
            fh.write(out)


class GdsCell:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.polygons = []   # (layer, datatype, [(x, y), ...], tag)
        self.labels = []     # (layer, texttype, (x, y), string)
        self.refs = []       # (cellname, (x, y))

    def rect(self, layer, datatype, x0, y0, x1, y1, tag=""):
        pts = [(x0, y0), (x1, y0), (x1, y1), (x0, y1)]
        self.polygons.append((layer, datatype, pts, tag))

    def label(self, layer, texttype, x, y, text):
        self.labels.append((layer, texttype, (x, y), text))

    def ref(self, cellname, x, y, mirror_x=False):
        """mirror_x: reflect about the y axis (GDS STRANS reflection + 180 deg) -- cell spans x-w..x when mirrored"""
        self.refs.append((cellname, (x, y), mirror_x))

    def to_bytes(self) -> bytes:
        out = bytearray()
        out += _record(BGNSTR, DT_INT2, _timestamp())
        out += _ascii(STRNAME, self.name)
        for layer, datatype, pts, _tag in self.polygons:
            out += _record(BOUNDARY, DT_NONE)
            out += _int2(LAYER, layer)
            out += _int2(DATATYPE, datatype)
            closed = list(pts) + [pts[0]]
            flat = [int(round(c)) for p in closed for c in p]
            out += _record(XY, DT_INT4, struct.pack(">%di" % len(flat), *flat))
            out += _record(ENDEL, DT_NONE)
        for layer, texttype, (x, y), text in self.labels:
            out += _record(TEXT, DT_NONE)
            out += _int2(LAYER, layer)
            out += _int2(TEXTTYPE, texttype)
            out += _record(PRESENTATION, DT_BITARRAY, struct.pack(">H", 0x0005))  # centre/centre
            out += _record(MAG, DT_REAL8, _real8(0.02))
            out += _record(XY, DT_INT4, struct.pack(">2i", int(x), int(y)))
            out += _ascii(STRING, text)
            out += _record(ENDEL, DT_NONE)
        for cellname, (x, y), *flags in self.refs:
            out += _record(SREF, DT_NONE)
            out += _ascii(SNAME, cellname)
            if flags and flags[0]:
                out += _record(STRANS, DT_BITARRAY, struct.pack(">H", 0x8000))
                out += _record(ANGLE, DT_REAL8, _real8(180.0))
            out += _record(XY, DT_INT4, struct.pack(">2i", int(x), int(y)))
            out += _record(ENDEL, DT_NONE)
        out += _record(ENDSTR, DT_NONE)
        return bytes(out)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Technology: generic 3-nm-class GAA nanosheet rules (nm)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TECH = dict(
    CPP=48,          # contacted poly (gate) pitch
    LG=14,           # physical gate length
    M1_PITCH=28,     # metal-1 pitch (6-track cell)
    TRACKS=6,
    NS_W_N=30,       # nanosheet width, NMOS
    NS_W_P=45,       # nanosheet width, PMOS (tuned for beta ratio)
    NS_T=5,          # nanosheet thickness
    NS_N=3,          # sheets in the stack
    NS_SPACE=9,      # vertical sheet-to-sheet spacing (inner spacer / gate fill)
    SD_W=20,         # source/drain trench contact width
    V0=10,           # via-0 size
    M1_W=16,         # metal-1 line width
    RAIL_W=24,       # power rail width (straddles cell boundary)
)
CELL_H = TECH["TRACKS"] * TECH["M1_PITCH"]      # 168 nm
CELL_W = 2 * TECH["CPP"]                       # 96 nm (single-gate cell + 2 half dummy gates)

# GDS layer map (layer, datatype) -- see gaa3.layermap
L = dict(
    NWELL=(1, 0), NSHEET=(2, 0), NS_STACK_MARK=(2, 1), GATE=(3, 0), GATE_CUT=(3, 1),
    SDC=(4, 0), CB=(5, 0), V0=(6, 0), M1=(7, 0), M1_PIN=(7, 1), M1_TEXT=(7, 2),
    PRBOUND=(235, 0),
)


def build_inverter() -> GdsCell:
    t = TECH
    c = GdsCell("INV_GAA_X1")
    xc = CELL_W // 2                      # gate centre
    lg2 = t["LG"] // 2

    # -- boundary and wells ----------------------------------------------------
    c.rect(*L["PRBOUND"], 0, 0, CELL_W, CELL_H, "prBoundary")
    c.rect(*L["NWELL"], 0, CELL_H // 2, CELL_W, CELL_H, "NWELL")

    # -- nanosheet stacks (active) ---------------------------------------------
    n_y0, n_y1 = 34, 34 + t["NS_W_N"]                      # NMOS sheet band (34..64)
    p_y1 = CELL_H - 34
    p_y0 = p_y1 - t["NS_W_P"]                              # PMOS sheet band (89..134)
    act_x0, act_x1 = 8, CELL_W - 8
    c.rect(*L["NSHEET"], act_x0, n_y0, act_x1, n_y1, "NS_N")
    c.rect(*L["NSHEET"], act_x0, p_y0, act_x1, p_y1, "NS_P")
    # stack-count marker (3 sheets) drawn as thin stripes for visualisation
    for i in range(t["NS_N"]):
        dy_n = n_y0 + 4 + i * ((t["NS_W_N"] - 8) // t["NS_N"])
        dy_p = p_y0 + 5 + i * ((t["NS_W_P"] - 10) // t["NS_N"])
        c.rect(*L["NS_STACK_MARK"], act_x0 + 2, dy_n, act_x1 - 2, dy_n + 2, "sheet")
        c.rect(*L["NS_STACK_MARK"], act_x0 + 2, dy_p, act_x1 - 2, dy_p + 2, "sheet")

    # -- gates: active gate + two half dummy (diffusion-break) gates -------------
    c.rect(*L["GATE"], xc - lg2, 14, xc + lg2, CELL_H - 14, "gate")
    c.rect(*L["GATE"], -lg2, 14, lg2, CELL_H - 14, "dummy")
    c.rect(*L["GATE"], CELL_W - lg2, 14, CELL_W + lg2, CELL_H - 14, "dummy")
    c.rect(*L["GATE_CUT"], 0, CELL_H // 2 - 4, CELL_W, CELL_H // 2 + 4, "cut (N/P share gate: no cut on active gate)")

    # -- source/drain trench contacts -----------------------------------------
    sd = t["SD_W"]
    src_x0 = xc - lg2 - 4 - sd          # 14..34
    drn_x0 = xc + lg2 + 10              # 65..85 (output bar 12 nm from the input pad)
    for (y0, y1) in ((n_y0 - 2, n_y1 + 2), (p_y0 - 2, p_y1 + 2)):
        c.rect(*L["SDC"], src_x0, y0, src_x0 + sd, y1, "S")
        c.rect(*L["SDC"], drn_x0, y0, drn_x0 + sd, y1, "D")

    # -- gate contact (CB) in the mid region between N and P sheets --------------
    c.rect(*L["CB"], xc - lg2 - 2, CELL_H // 2 - 8, xc + lg2 + 2, CELL_H // 2 + 8, "CB")

    # -- metal-1 -----------------------------------------------------------------
    m1 = t["M1_W"]
    rw = t["RAIL_W"] // 2
    c.rect(*L["M1"], -4, -rw, CELL_W + 4, rw, "VSS rail")
    c.rect(*L["M1"], -4, CELL_H - rw, CELL_W + 4, CELL_H + rw, "VDD rail")
    # source straps to rails
    sx = src_x0 + sd // 2
    c.rect(*L["M1"], sx - m1 // 2, 0, sx + m1 // 2, n_y1, "VSS strap")
    c.rect(*L["M1"], sx - m1 // 2, CELL_H // 2 + 20, sx + m1 // 2, CELL_H, "VDD strap")   # starts 12 nm above the A pad
    # output: vertical M1 joining N and P drains
    dx = drn_x0 + sd // 2
    c.rect(*L["M1"], dx - m1 // 2, n_y0, dx + m1 // 2, p_y1, "Y")
    c.rect(*L["M1_PIN"], dx - m1 // 2, CELL_H // 2 - 8, dx + m1 // 2, CELL_H // 2 + 8, "Y pin")
    # input: M1 landing pad over gate contact
    c.rect(*L["M1"], xc - 9, CELL_H // 2 - 8, xc + 7, CELL_H // 2 + 8, "A")            # 16-nm pad, 12 nm from the Y bar
    c.rect(*L["M1_PIN"], xc - 9, CELL_H // 2 - 8, xc + 7, CELL_H // 2 + 8, "A pin")

    # -- via-0 --------------------------------------------------------------------
    v = t["V0"] // 2
    for (x, y) in ((sx, (n_y0 + n_y1) // 2), (sx, (p_y0 + p_y1) // 2 + 1),   # P source via 1 nm up: enclosed by the shortened strap
                   (dx, (n_y0 + n_y1) // 2), (dx, (p_y0 + p_y1) // 2),
                   (xc - 1, CELL_H // 2)):
        c.rect(*L["V0"], x - v, y - v, x + v, y + v, "V0")

    # -- pin labels ---------------------------------------------------------------
    c.label(*L["M1_TEXT"], xc - 1, CELL_H // 2, "A")
    c.label(*L["M1_TEXT"], dx, CELL_H // 2, "Y")
    c.label(*L["M1_TEXT"], CELL_W // 2, CELL_H, "VDD")
    c.label(*L["M1_TEXT"], CELL_W // 2, 0, "VSS")
    return c


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. SVG renderer (same polygons, GDS-viewer style)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
STYLE = {  # layer -> (fill, stroke, opacity)
    (235, 0): ("none", "#8a8f98", 1.0),
    (1, 0): ("#c9b458", "#a08b2e", 0.22),
    (2, 0): ("#4caf50", "#2e7d32", 0.55),
    (2, 1): ("#1b5e20", "#1b5e20", 0.9),
    (3, 0): ("#e53935", "#b71c1c", 0.75),
    (3, 1): ("none", "#b71c1c", 0.9),
    (4, 0): ("#9e9e9e", "#616161", 0.9),
    (5, 0): ("#212121", "#000000", 0.9),
    (6, 0): ("#ffffff", "#000000", 1.0),
    (7, 0): ("#1e88e5", "#0d47a1", 0.62),
    (7, 1): ("none", "#0d47a1", 1.0),
}


def to_svg(cell: GdsCell, pad=20, scale=3.0) -> str:
    xs = [p[0] for _, _, pts, _ in cell.polygons for p in pts]
    ys = [p[1] for _, _, pts, _ in cell.polygons for p in pts]
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = min(xs) - pad, max(xs) + pad, min(ys) - pad, max(ys) + pad
    w, h = (x1 - x0) * scale, (y1 - y0) * scale

    def X(x): return (x - x0) * scale
    def Y(y): return (y1 - y) * scale  # flip: GDS y up, SVG y down

    order = [(1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 1), (3, 0), (3, 1), (4, 0), (5, 0), (7, 0), (6, 0), (7, 1), (235, 0)]
    parts = [f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 {w:.0f} {h:.0f}" '
             f'width="{w:.0f}" height="{h:.0f}" font-family="ui-monospace, monospace">']
    parts.append('<defs><pattern id="hatch" width="6" height="6" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse" '
                 'patternTransform="rotate(45)"><rect width="6" height="6" fill="#e53935" opacity="0.35"/>'
                 '<line x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="6" stroke="#b71c1c" stroke-width="1.5"/></pattern></defs>')
    for key in order:
        for layer, dt, pts, tag in cell.polygons:
            if (layer, dt) != key:
                continue
            fill, stroke, op = STYLE[key]
            if key == (3, 0):
                fill = "url(#hatch)"
            d = " ".join(f"{X(x):.1f},{Y(y):.1f}" for x, y in pts)
            dash = ' stroke-dasharray="4 3"' if key in ((235, 0), (3, 1), (7, 1)) else ""
            parts.append(f'<polygon points="{d}" fill="{fill}" fill-opacity="{op}" stroke="{stroke}" '
                         f'stroke-width="1"{dash}><title>L{layer}:{dt} {tag}</title></polygon>')
    for layer, tt, (x, y), text in cell.labels:
        parts.append(f'<text x="{X(x):.1f}" y="{Y(y) + 4:.1f}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" '
                     f'font-weight="700" fill="#111">{text}</text>')
    parts.append("</svg>")
    return "\n".join(parts)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    lib = GdsLibrary("GAA3_INV_LIB")
    inv = build_inverter()
    lib.cells.append(inv)
    lib.write("gaa_inverter.gds")
    with open("gaa_inverter.svg", "w") as fh:
        fh.write(to_svg(inv))
    with open("gaa_inverter_polygons.json", "w") as fh:
        json.dump(dict(tech=TECH, cell_w_nm=CELL_W, cell_h_nm=CELL_H,
                       polygons=[dict(layer=l, datatype=d, tag=t, xy=p) for l, d, p, t in inv.polygons],
                       labels=[dict(layer=l, texttype=t, xy=xy, text=s) for l, t, xy, s in inv.labels]),
                  fh, indent=1)
    n_poly = len(inv.polygons)
    print(f"wrote gaa_inverter.gds  cell {inv.name}  {CELL_W}x{CELL_H} nm  {n_poly} polygons  "
          f"{len(inv.labels)} labels  area {CELL_W*CELL_H/1e6:.4f} um^2")

# GAA Nanosheet Inverter: Cadence RTL-to-GDSII Flow

Design and implementation of a gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet CMOS inverter
(`INV_GAA_X1`, 3-nm-class generic rules) with a complete Cadence flow:

| Stage | Tool (VMware guest) | Script | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Device / cell design | Virtuoso Schematic + Spectre (BSIM-CMG) | `spectre/gaa_inv_tb.scs` | VTC, delay, power |
| Cell layout | Virtuoso Layout XL, Pegasus/PVS DRC-LVS | `layout/gen_gaa_inverter_gds.py`, `layout/streamout_virtuoso.il` | `layout/gaa_inverter.gds` |
| RTL | Xcelium | `rtl/inverter.v`, `rtl/inverter_tb.v` | simulation log |
| Synthesis | Genus | `genus/synth.tcl`, `genus/constraints.sdc` | mapped netlist, SDF |
| Place & route | Innovus | `innovus/pnr.tcl`, `innovus/mmmc.tcl` | DEF, SPEF, **`inverter.gds`** |
| NAND2 cell | Spectre, Genus/Innovus, Python | `spectre/gaa_nand2_tb.scs`, `rtl/nand2.v`, `spectre/nand2.py`, `layout/gen_gaa_nand2_gds.py` | `results_nand2*.json`, `layout/gaa_nand2.gds` |
| 6T SRAM bitcell | Spectre, Python | `spectre/gaa_sram6t_tb.scs`, `spectre/sram6t.py`, `layout/gen_gaa_sram6t_gds.py` | `results_sram6t*.json`, `layout/gaa_sram6t.gds` |
| RTL-to-GDSII (reference) | Python | `flow/gaa3_lib.py`, `flow/genus_ref.py`, `flow/innovus_ref.py` | `flow/lib/*.lib,*.lef`, `flow/out/*_netlist.v, *.def, *.gds`, `flow/reports/*` |
| DRC / LVS | Pegasus (sign-off), Python+gdstk (reference) | `verify/gaa3_drc.py`, `verify/gaa3_lvs.py`, `verify/run_all.sh` | `verify/*.drc.sum`, `verify/*.lvs.rpt` (all cells DRC-clean, LVS MATCH) |
| Reference check | Python (no deps) | `spectre/ref_model.py` | `results.json`, SVG figures |
| Ring oscillator | Spectre, Genus, Python | `spectre/gaa_ro11_tb.scs`, `rtl/ring_osc.v`, `genus/synth_ro.tcl`, `spectre/ro.py`, `layout/gen_gaa_ro_gds.py` | `results_ro*.json`, `layout/gaa_ro11.gds` |

`layout/gaa_inverter.gds` is a valid Calma GDSII stream (1 nm database unit,
library `GAA3_INV_LIB`, cell `INV_GAA_X1`, 32 boundaries, 4 pin texts).
It was written by the dependency-free writer in `gen_gaa_inverter_gds.py`
and read back with `gdstk`.

## 1. VMware Workstation host setup

1. Create a VM: Linux guest (RHEL 8.x / Rocky 8 / CentOS 7.9 are on the Cadence
   support matrix), 4+ vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 120 GB thin-provisioned disk, NAT network.
2. Install VMware Tools / open-vm-tools and enable a shared folder that maps
   this repository into the guest (`/mnt/hgfs/gaa_inverter`).
3. Install the Cadence tools from the IC/DDI/Genus/Innovus/Xcelium installers,
   then set the licence server:
   ```bash
   export CDS_LIC_FILE=5280@license-host      # or LM_LICENSE_FILE
   export CDSHOME=/opt/cadence/IC231
   export GAA3_LIB=/opt/pdk/gaa3               # generic GAA kit: liberty, lef, gds, qrc
   export PATH=$CDSHOME/tools/bin:$CDSHOME/tools/dfII/bin:/opt/cadence/GENUS231/bin:/opt/cadence/INNOVUS231/bin:/opt/cadence/XCELIUM2309/bin:$PATH
   ```
4. Snapshot the VM after installation so a broken flow can be rolled back.

## 2. Cell-level flow (Virtuoso / Spectre)

```bash
cd spectre && spectre gaa_inv_tb.scs +log spectre.log       # BSIM-CMG nanosheet models
python3 ref_model.py                                        # reference metrics for cross-check
GAA_TECH=finfet python3 ref_model.py                        # 5-nm-class FinFET baseline (Table V)
python3 ro.py && GAA_TECH=finfet python3 ro.py && python3 ro.py --figs   # RO11 FO3 sweep (Table VI)
spectre gaa_ro11_tb.scs +log ro.log                         # RO11 in Spectre
python3 nand2.py && GAA_TECH=finfet python3 nand2.py       # NAND2 static/transient/leakage (Table VII)
cd ../layout && python3 gen_gaa_ro_gds.py                   # hierarchical RO11 GDSII
python3 gen_gaa_nand2_gds.py                                # NAND2_GAA_X1 GDSII
python3 gen_gaa_sram6t_gds.py                               # SRAM6T_GAA_HD GDSII
cd ../spectre && GAA_TECH=finfet python3 sram6t.py && python3 sram6t.py   # SRAM SNM / write / read (Table VIII)
```
In Virtuoso: `File > Import > Stream` the GDS in `layout/` (layer map
`layout/gaa3.layermap`) to obtain the `INV_GAA_X1 layout` cellview, run DRC/LVS,
then `File > Export > Stream` (or `load("streamout_virtuoso.il")`) to regenerate GDSII.

## 3. RTL-to-GDSII flow (Xcelium / Genus / Innovus)

```bash
cd rtl     && xrun -timescale 1ps/1fs inverter.v inverter_tb.v
cd ../genus   && genus   -files synth.tcl -log logs/genus
cd ../innovus && innovus -init  pnr.tcl   -log logs/innovus
# -> innovus/out/inverter.gds (merged with the standard-cell GDS)
```

## 3b. Reference RTL-to-GDSII run (no licence needed)

```bash
cd flow && python3 gaa3_lib.py && python3 genus_ref.py inverter nand2 ring_osc && python3 innovus_ref.py inverter nand2 ring_osc
```

## 4. Verifying the GDSII

```bash
./verify/run_all.sh      # regenerates the four cells, runs the 26-rule GAA3 DRC and the LVS extraction
```


```bash
python3 -c "import gdstk; l=gdstk.read_gds('layout/gaa_inverter.gds'); \
  c=l.cells[0]; print(c.name, len(c.polygons), c.bounding_box())"
klayout layout/gaa_inverter.gds        # optional viewer
```

All numbers in `spectre/results.json` come from the Python reference model,
not from a Spectre run; replace them with the extracted Spectre/Innovus
values after running the flow in the VMware guest.
